label: Read Inkling 2 Mini, then run it

recall.prompt: Why can two equally long strings consume different numbers of tokens?
rubric: Tokenization maps strings to vocabulary IDs.
Vocabulary and text segmentation vary.

recall.prompt: What changes when you give a model a prompt rather than train it?
rubric: Inputs and intermediate activations change during inference.
Weights remain fixed unless a training or adaptation operation updates them.

recall.prompt: Why are two different four-bit formats not necessarily interchangeable?
rubric: They can encode different values and scaling rules.
Kernels must support the encoding.

recall.prompt: How does an embedding differ from a token ID?
rubric: An ID identifies a vocabulary entry.
An embedding is a vector used in computation or similarity.

recall.prompt: Distinguish weights from activations in a network.
rubric: Weights persist across requests.
Activations depend on the input and execution.

recall.prompt: What are the roles of the loss, gradient, and optimizer?
rubric: Loss defines an objective.
Gradient gives local sensitivity.
Optimizer applies an update.

recall.prompt: Why does a causal decoder mask future tokens?
rubric: Prevent access to future targets during prediction.
Match the autoregressive dependency structure.

recall.prompt: What does a transformer layer do that a tokenizer does not?
rubric: Transforms vector representations using attention and feed-forward operations.
A tokenizer maps text to IDs.

recall.prompt: What is the output of one next-token prediction before sampling?
rubric: A set of scores or probabilities over the vocabulary.
A decoding rule chooses a token.

recall.prompt: Why can a pretrained model complete text but struggle to follow chat instructions?
rubric: Its original objective is prediction, not necessarily instruction following.
Post-training can improve instruction behavior.

recall.prompt: Does running a model repeatedly teach it new facts permanently?
rubric: Ordinary inference does not update weights.
External memory or a new prompt can change later inputs.

recall.prompt: Why might a model advertising a very long context still run poorly on a laptop?
rubric: KV cache and other runtime allocations grow with context.
Hardware and runtime limits may be lower than the architecture maximum.

recall.prompt: What work does a KV cache save, and what does it cost?
rubric: Reuse previous keys and values.
Consumes memory as cached positions grow.

recall.prompt: Why should prompt tokens per second and generation tokens per second be reported separately?
rubric: They measure distinct processing phases.
Different sequence shapes and bottlenecks affect them.

recall.prompt: Can decode tokens per second alone determine end-to-end latency?
rubric: No: loading, prefill, token count and overhead matter.
Time to first token needs separate measurement.

recall.prompt: Why might a 20 GB model fail on a machine with 32 GB unified memory?
rubric: Other applications and runtime overhead share the pool.
KV cache and working buffers consume additional memory.

recall.prompt: Estimate raw storage for 8 billion weights at four bits, ignoring overhead.
rubric: About 4 GB in decimal units.
Actual file size and peak RAM can be larger.

recall.prompt: Why is a model trained in a low-bit format different from one converted to four bits afterward?
rubric: Training can adapt to the format’s rounding and scaling.
Post-training conversion may introduce additional error.
Runtime support is separate.

recall.prompt: Why are active parameters not a valid estimate of model file size?
rubric: Inactive experts still have stored weights.
Routing chooses a subset per token.

recall.prompt: A model has 26.4B total and 3.4B active parameters. Which count is closer to the starting point for weight storage?
rubric: Total parameter count.
Active count describes work, not all stored weights.
Precision and overhead still matter.

recall.prompt: A 24-layer model repeats its middle 12 layers three times. How many layer applications occur per token?
rubric: 48 = 12 non-repeated + 36 repeated applications.
Only 24 distinct stored layers.

recall.prompt: Why might a learned gate help when adding loops during training?
rubric: Initially restricts the new recurrent signal.
Can gradually learn to admit useful information.
Does not guarantee stable training in every model.

recall.prompt: What tradeoff follows expert pruning?
rubric: Lower stored parameter count.
Potential performance loss requiring measurement or recovery.

recall.prompt: How is distillation different from copying teacher weights?
rubric: The student learns from teacher-generated targets or signals.
Weights are optimized rather than simply copied.

recall.prompt: What evidence would demonstrate successful healing?
rubric: Compare pre-prune, post-prune, and healed performance.
Use comparable held-out tasks and settings.

recall.prompt: When would fine-tuning be preferable to adding instructions to every request?
rubric: Repeated stable behavior or format across examples.
Adequate training data and held-out evals.
Not a default store for frequently changing facts.

recall.prompt: Why hold out examples when training with SFT?
rubric: Training examples can be memorized.
Held-out examples test generalization.

recall.prompt: How do SFT and RL differ in their training signals?
rubric: SFT uses target demonstrations.
RL uses rewards on sampled actions or trajectories.

recall.prompt: What makes distillation on-policy?
rubric: Student samples its current policy’s states or trajectories.
Teacher signal guides learning on those samples.

recall.prompt: Does a shorter written reasoning trace imply less internal computation?
rubric: No; computation per token can differ.
Trace length is not a complete measure of internal work.

recall.prompt: What must be held constant before attributing a benchmark improvement to the model?
rubric: Comparable tasks, scoring and harness.
Comparable budgets and inference settings.
Report uncertainty or repeated trials.

recall.prompt: Why might the same checkpoint get different coding scores in different harnesses?
rubric: Tool access, context and retries differ.
Execution and scoring may differ.

recall.prompt: A price list changes weekly. Would you retrain or retrieve it at runtime first?
rubric: Retrieve current version with provenance.
No weight update required.
Evaluate grounding and access controls.

recall.prompt: How could a model produce fewer tokens yet do more computation per token?
rubric: Repeat internal layers.
Token count and internal compute are separate quantities.
Measure wall-clock and quality too.

recall.prompt: Does legible reasoning establish that a monitor can catch all harmful behavior?
rubric: No: legibility differs from faithfulness and detection.
Detection depends on the monitor and test setting.

recall.prompt: How does an activation intervention differ from reading a reasoning trace?
rubric: It probes or changes internal computation.
Written traces are observable outputs, not complete internal records.

recall.prompt: What does it mean to estimate that a baseline needs more compute to match held-out loss?
rubric: Compare at equal held-out loss rather than equal steps.
A fitted scaling relationship supports the estimate.
Do not equate training compute with decode speed.

recall.prompt: If a no-CoT time horizon rises, does the model take that many seconds to respond?
rubric: No; the unit describes human task duration.
It is a fitted accuracy threshold.
Compare only under a common protocol.

recall.prompt: Why can lower trace controllability be interesting without proving improved safety?
rubric: It may make some instructed trace manipulation harder.
It does not establish that all relevant internal behavior is observable.

recall.prompt: Can a model accept images without generating images?
rubric: Yes; input and output modalities are distinct.
A vision encoder can supply representations for text generation.

recall.prompt: Explain how this model trades stored weights, computation per token, training choices, and visible reasoning for laptop inference.
rubric: Separate stored weights from weight activations.
Explain shared-loop depth and low-bit storage.
Explain pruning and healing.
Distinguish reported results from causal or universal safety claims.
Account for local RAM and runtime limitations.
